clue.text: Bad-tempered bunch mostly unknown to attend church

indicators.note: mostly means the word for bunch loses its final letter

parts.note: a bunch is a group
Y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A grumpy crowd, nearly all strangers, turns up for a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the last letter of the word for a bunch; 'to attend' just sets the unknown after church, so the clue's order is not the answer's.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: someone grouchy is irritable and cross.

clue.text: Idols displayed in gallery

definitions.meaning: the highest gallery in a theatre is nicknamed this

explanation.surface: Statues of idols on show in an art gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: In British theatres the top balcony, the cheapest seats, is called 'the gods'.
explanation.definitionFit: Deities are idols; and the topmost theatre gallery bears this nickname.

clue.text: Supervise deliveries — get it?

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled, or deliveries
see? means do you understand?

explanation.surface: A manager checks on parcels and asks if they have arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: An over in cricket is a series of six deliveries by one bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: to oversee is to supervise work or workers.

clue.text: Something pear-shaped almost? That's funny

indicators.note: almost means the pear name stops one letter short

parts.note: Comice is a variety of pear, so literally pear-shaped

explanation.surface: A disaster narrowly avoided turns out to be amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pear-shaped' is British slang for gone wrong, but here it is a pear itself, the Comice, cut short by 'almost'.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: comic means amusing, causing laughter.

clue.text: The old, old woman accommodating new cavalrymen once

parts.note: ye is an archaic spelling of the

indicators.note: accommodating means holding inside, so the woman's name contains the new letter

parts.note: Mary is a woman's name

explanation.surface: An elderly woman puts up some new mounted soldiers in times past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The old' is the archaic article written with a Y; 'accommodating' puts the new letter inside the woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The yeomanry were volunteer cavalry forces raised from farmers in Britain.

clue.text: Story line following horse in training

indicators.note: in places the horse and line inside the training abbreviation

parts.note: PE is physical education, physical training at school

indicators.note: following puts the line letter after the horse

parts.note: an Arab is a breed of horse

explanation.surface: A tale about a racing line taken behind a horse being trained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' sets the line letter after the horse, and 'in' puts both inside the school abbreviation for physical training.
explanation.definitionFit: A parable is a short moral tale, a kind of story.

clue.text: Coup placed educational establishment at the bottom

indicators.note: at the bottom means the school letters come below in this down entry

parts.note: put means placed
SCH is the abbreviation for school

explanation.surface: A coup put a school at the bottom of the league.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at the bottom' puts SCH beneath PUT in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A putsch is a sudden attempt to overthrow a government.

clue.text: Around university his glory is demolished in a playful way

indicators.note: Around means the scrambled letters surround the university letter
is demolished means the words are knocked down and rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A student's reputation is wrecked by campus pranks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is demolished' rearranges HIS GLORY and 'Around' wraps the result about U.
explanation.definitionFit: Roguishly means mischievously, with playful naughtiness.

clue.text: Henry of Navarre, for one, takes the biscuit!

definitions.meaning: Henry IV of France, first king of the French royal house of that name
a chocolate sandwich biscuit popular in Britain

explanation.surface: A French king wins the prize, or is outrageous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes the biscuit' is a British idiom for being outrageous; here it links the royal house to a British chocolate cream biscuit.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry IV founded the Bourbon dynasty; a Bourbon is also a chocolate sandwich biscuit.

clue.text: More senior bishop visiting Turkish governor's wine supplier

parts.note: elder means older, more senior

indicators.note: visiting means going inside, so the bishop goes into the governor

parts.note: a bey was a governor in the Ottoman Empire
RR, Right Reverend, is a bishop's title

explanation.surface: A senior bishop calls on a Turkish official who provides the wine.
explanation.walkthrough: RR, the abbreviation of Right Reverend, goes inside BEY.
explanation.definitionFit: Elderberries are fermented into country wine, so the berry supplies it.

clue.text: A drab tome oddly captivating person of opposite sex

indicators.note: oddly signals that the letters of the preceding words are arranged in a strange way

explanation.surface: A dull book somehow wins over an attractive admirer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' looks like a call for alternate letters, but here it scrambles A DRAB TOME.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal term for a very attractive person one fancies, typically a man.

clue.text: Fleshy fruit man pinched from glutton

indicators.note: pinched from means stolen out of, so these letters are removed

parts.note: a gourmand is a greedy eater
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man filches some soft fruit from a greedy eater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pinched from' removes MAN from GOURMAND.
explanation.definitionFit: A gourd is the large fleshy fruit of plants such as squash and pumpkin.

clue.text: Upstart party member visiting rejected play area

parts.note: a social is a party or gathering

indicators.note: visiting puts the member inside the other piece, as a guest goes in
rejected means the play area word is turned back to front

parts.note: REC, short for recreation ground, is a British public playing field
a limb is a member of the body

explanation.surface: An unwelcome party member drops in at a playground nobody wants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns the play area round to CER, and 'visiting' puts the body member inside. A rec is a British recreation ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe someone trying to rise above their station; an upstart has risen too fast.

clue.text: Move around screen, having argument over king's decorative art

parts.note: to scroll is to move text up and down a computer screen

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the argument word is read backwards

parts.note: a row is an argument
K is the abbreviation for king, as in chess

explanation.surface: Browsing a screen after a quarrel about royal decorations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns ROW into WOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrollwork is ornamental carving or design based on spiral shapes.

clue.text: Game identifying Bucks country house?

definitions.meaning: the Prime Minister's official country residence in Buckinghamshire

explanation.surface: Playing a game that reveals which manor in the Home Counties it is.
explanation.walkthrough: Bucks is short for Buckinghamshire, an English county; Chequers is the British Prime Minister's country house there.
explanation.definitionFit: A proper name for the PM's retreat and also the board game known in the US as checkers.

clue.text: Remove cover from a French novel devoured around hospital

parts.note: un is French for a
She is a novel by H. Rider Haggard

indicators.note: around means the eating word goes round the hospital letter

parts.note: ate means devoured

explanation.surface: Uncovering a French paperback eaten up in hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' is Rider Haggard's adventure novel; 'around' puts ATE round H, giving ATHE.
explanation.definitionFit: To unsheathe is to draw a blade from its scabbard, removing its cover.

clue.text: It may be small, but we vary our routine for one

definitions.meaning: small ... means coins of low value

definitions.text: we vary our routine for one
definitions.meaning: doing something different for a ..., for variety

explanation.surface: A modest thing that prompts us to break our habits.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half recalls 'small change', loose coins; the second recalls doing something 'for a change'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: coins in the pocket, and a departure from the usual.

clue.text: Blooming action required in tiddlywinks!

definitions.meaning: a mild British intensifier like damned
the counters are flicked over in this game

explanation.surface: A frustrated cry about the fiddly business of a children's game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' and its equivalent are mild British oaths; in tiddlywinks small discs are made to jump by pressing their edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: a polite British swear word, and the act of flicking counters over.

clue.text: But were the Angles so boneheaded?

definitions.meaning: an angle wider than a right angle is so described, punning on the Angles, an old Germanic tribe

explanation.surface: A historian asks whether the Anglo-Saxon settlers were really so dim.
explanation.walkthrough: The Angles were a people who settled England; read as geometry, an angle over 90 degrees has this name.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: an obtuse person is dull and slow to understand.

clue.text: Blast and flay a sailor first

indicators.note: first puts the sailor before the a

parts.note: to tan someone is to beat or flay them
tar is an old word for a sailor

explanation.surface: A curse, then a call to whip a seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blast' looks like an oath but is a trumpet sound; 'first' sets TAR ahead of A.
explanation.definitionFit: A tantara is a fanfare or blast on a trumpet.

clue.text: Person in theatre: member of team about to operate?

indicators.note: about means going round, so the team member surrounds the other piece

parts.note: a player is a member of a team
to go is to work or operate, as a machine does

explanation.surface: Someone in the operating theatre: a team member ready to begin surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'theatre' and 'operate' suggest surgery, but the theatre here is the stage kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A playgoer is someone who attends the theatre.

clue.text: Irishwoman and daughter in drama in Florida city

parts.note: Orla is an Irish girl's name

indicators.note: in places the daughter inside the drama word

parts.note: Noh, also spelt No, is classical Japanese drama

explanation.surface: An Irish mother and daughter acting in a play in Florida.
explanation.walkthrough: No (or Noh) is Japanese masked drama; D goes 'in' it, giving NDO.
explanation.definitionFit: Orlando is a city in central Florida, home to Disney World.

clue.text: Swaying unsteadily, one may be thrown in temper

definitions.text: one may be thrown in temper
definitions.meaning: to throw a fit of temper, a tantrum, in British slang

explanation.surface: Someone tottering about, likely to be tossed in a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'throw a wobbly' is British slang for having a tantrum.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: unstable on its feet, and a tantrum.

clue.text: NCO cut exam, securing my permission at first

parts.note: to lance is to cut open, as a boil
cor is an exclamation of surprise, like my!

indicators.note: at first takes only the opening letter of permission

parts.note: an oral is a spoken examination; securing only ties it on to the pieces before it

explanation.surface: A junior officer skips a test after getting the nod from someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'my' as an exclamation gives the British COR; 'at first' takes P from 'permission'. 'securing' is only loosely a link: the exam is fastened on after those pieces, not around them.
explanation.definitionFit: A lance corporal is the lowest rank of non-commissioned officer in the British Army.

clue.text: Again provide weaponry for state changing sides at one point

indicators.note: one letter for left is swapped for its opposite, right

parts.note: a realm is a kingdom or state

explanation.surface: A country swaps alliances and arms up again.
explanation.walkthrough: L (left) in REALM becomes R (right).
explanation.definitionFit: To rearm is to equip with weapons once more.

clue.text: First officer winning position on

definitions.meaning: a ship's first officer, below the captain

explanation.surface: A deputy captain is in a winning position.
explanation.walkthrough: On a merchant ship the first officer is called the first mate.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: a ship's deputy officer, and the final winning position in chess.

clue.text: One's initial role in abstract painting

indicators.note: initial means only the first letter of the word one is used

parts.note: a part is a role in a play

explanation.surface: A painter's first role is in abstract art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initial' takes O from 'One's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Op art is a style of abstract painting using optical illusions.

clue.text: In a barn it forged a type of metal

indicators.note: forged means shaped or made up, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A blacksmith works some metal in a farm building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forged' scrambles IN A BARN IT; it suits the metalworking picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Britannia metal is a pewter-like alloy of tin, antimony and copper.

clue.text: Rascally behaviour of church body in Kerry, oddly

indicators.note: in places the church body inside the selected letters
oddly takes the letters in odd positions of the county name

parts.note: the nave is the main body of a church

explanation.surface: Mischief by a church group in County Kerry, strangely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' takes K, R, Y from Kerry, an Irish county, and NAVE goes 'in' them.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: knavery is dishonest, roguish conduct.

clue.text: Yellow, but willing to cross marshy ground

indicators.note: to cross means to straddle, so the willing word spans the marshy ground

parts.note: game means willing, up for it
a bog is marshy ground

explanation.surface: Cowardly, but prepared to wade across a swamp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yellow' tempts as cowardice, but it is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamboge is a deep yellow pigment from a gum resin.
